The main takeaway from our work is that

QS regulation of siderophore biosynthesis is more complex than previously thought, and that siderophores produced by QS regulation are not only cell-associated, as is often assumed, but can also be present at very high concentrations in the environment.

QS regulation of siderophore biosynthesis is not a “black box” and that siderophore production and uptake can be studied in detail to better understand the role of these small molecules in bacterial growth and survival.

QS regulation of siderophores can help bacteria avoid overproduction of siderophores in excess of cellular Fe uptake capacities, an observation that is relevant to the study of siderophore-mediated virulence.
